title: Eisai
hookLine: brings Rinzai Zen and tea seeds back from China

lines: A BOWL OF TEA AND A LITTLE BOOK.
cards: The young shogun, in his capital at Kamakura, has a terrible morning after a night of drinking.
Someone is sent for, and a Buddhist monk arrives carrying two things: a bowl of tea, and a little book he has written about tea and health.
The shogun drinks, and, according to a chronicle of the time, feels better, and is pleased with the book. It is a small scene.
But the monk carrying the bowl had brought home from China a lineage of Zen practice and, tradition says, the seeds of tea plants too. His name was Eisai.

teach.b: First, the journey. Eisai was trained as a monk in the Tendai school on Mount Hiei, the same mountain where Honen studied.
He traveled to China looking for the living roots of the teaching, and there he received the Linji line of Chan.
In Japanese, Linji is pronounced Rinzai. So the true person of no rank, from a few days ago, comes home with him. Tradition remembers Eisai as the one who brought Rinzai Zen to Japan.

teach.h: TEA SEEDS, AND A BOOK ON TEA.
teach.b: Second, the seeds. Tradition also says he carried tea seeds back from China and planted them, and that tea gardens grew from them. Whether every story about those seeds is exact, his love of tea is in his own words.
Third, the book. He wrote a short work on drinking tea for health, the Kissa Yojoki. It opens by calling tea a wonderful medicine for nourishing life.
For him, tea was medicine first, a way to keep the body well. It was practical, not decorative. Fourth, the pair.
Eisai also wrote in defense of Zen, arguing that its practice could serve and protect the country.

teach.h: TWO GIFTS: SITTING AND A CUP.
teach.b: So he came home with two gifts that would, over time, grow into each other: a way of sitting, and a way of drinking a cup.

how: In Rinzai Zen temples, tea is served as part of the daily schedule and at ceremonies, and the tea ceremony that later developed in Japan kept close ties to Zen.

practice: Feel the weight of your body on the seat, then check in with it the way a careful doctor might: the shoulders, the eyes, the belly, the throat. Is anything tired, tight or thirsty?
Don't fix it yet; just notice what the body is asking for, one breath at a time.

wordCard.voice: Eisai. The Japanese monk tradition remembers for bringing Rinzai Zen, and tea, home from China. Today's word.
